newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK royals try to relaunch after decade "horribilis".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK royals try to relaunch after decade "horribilis".

text.p: Think of the British royal family and divorce, adultery and scandal leap to mind.

Around the queen circle a tortured son desperate to be king and unruly princesses known to overeat and overspend. The patriarch is frosty, outspoken to the point of rudeness and appears to hold little sway over a family that has run wild.
After fairytale weddings, the detritus of broken marriages litters the landscape and opinion polls show growing support for republicanism as secrets spill and traditions lapse.
Forget the queen's famous "annus horribilis" -- it has been an awful decade for Elizabeth. Faced with such ugly truths, the House of Windsor is belatedly trying to restore order.

Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip this year celebrate 50 years of marriage, hoping that a series of spectacular golden wedding events might draw a line under the problems and rekindle the happy family picture of old.
There will be a garden party at Buckingham Palace for other couples celebrating 50 years of matrimony, and a reception of thanks at Windsor Castle.
There are plans to cut the cost of running the royal palaces and to make regal travel less lavish, all in a drive to present a better face to the world.
AFTER NEW LABOUR, THE NEW ROYALS?

Attempts at a makeover are well timed, for Britons are in a strangely upbeat mood, full of hope about a new Labour government, a strong economy and London's reputation as the most happening city in the world.
"After new Labour, are we now about to witness the emergence of the new royals, sharing and caring alike?" the Guardian newspaper asked in an editorial.
Even Princess Diana and Prince Charles are trying, in fits and starts, to bury the hatchet and rebuild new lives now they are free of each other.
The daily round of vicious tabloid stories about their marriage breakup is over, but nobody expects glowing headlines after so much public acrimony.
Already, as they both carve out new images and roles, strains are showing amid the successes.

Diana scored points by selling old frocks for charity and nobody doubts her commitment to the dispossessed even as she bids to crown herself "Queen of Hearts" and lobbies to be a roving ambassador for Britain.
Charles, too, is poised to profit from his pet projects as he shares many social concerns with the new Labour government and is said to enjoy good relations with Prime Minister Tony Blair.
IMPERIOUS AND IDIOSYNCRATIC ODDBALL
Yet the public has never warmed to Charles.
His crusades are seen as the oddball hobbies of a middle-aged man without a proper job and his imperious manner and idiosyncratic taste alienate many.

Despite years of on and off courtship, he has failed to win public acceptance for his lover Camilla Parker Bowles and even his worthy initiatives for the young meet with criticism or, at best, coldness.

The Church gets cross because he doesn't go enough -- as king he would be head of the Church of England -- and teachers fume because he says in public what everybody fears in private about the state of schools.

"Prince Charles is ill-placed to condemn failure in others. One of the biggest problems teachers face in trying to raise standards is the poor behaviour so often produced by youngsters from broken homes," said union leader Nigel de Gruchy.
"His own spectacular failure in that area should lead him to maintain a decent silence on such issues."
A decade ago, few could have imagined such bald criticism of a future king.
"EXOCET" DIANA RILES ESTABLISHMENT
Diana, too, courts trouble.
Far more popular than her ex-husband, she has angered the establishment by appearing to meddle in politics and failing to behave with the dignity expected of a princess.
Columnists berate her unpredictability -- "What the hell will Exocet Di do next?" asked one -- while even her fans admit she lacks judgement.

Diana was forced to apologise twice in a week for marching into a landmines debate, breaching the old rule that royals and politics don't mix, and for taking her under-age son to a film sympathetic to guerrillas of the Irish Republican Army (IRA).
Yet Diana and Charles both crave public acceptance for themselves and a veneer of harmony for their sons.
Already the divorcees have attended some family events together and there is talk of official engagements later this year as a pair, if not a couple.
The Sunday Times said Charles "is concerned about trying to preserve the institution for the next generation" as royal ratings slump.

He is also being groomed to take over some duties from his mother, including overseas state visits, and represented the queen at last month's high-profile handover of power in Hong Kong to the Chinese.
The Daily Mail said a five-year plan would be launched at the palace to persuade Britons that Charles was not only "the people's prince" but fit to be king.
The moment of truth will not come until 2002, when the queen will celebrate 50 years on the throne and delegate more to her son.
Until then, an impatient Charles must bide his time, turn 50 with dignity and eye the throne with envy.
"With support for the royal family seriously weakened by what are perceived to be the prince's personal failings, his behaviour is now at the heart of the monarchy's future," the newspaper said.
